structures.name: Femoral Artery
structures.function: Main artery of the lower limb; continuation of external iliac below inguinal ligament; palpable in femoral triangle; passes through adductor canal (Hunter's canal) to become popliteal artery
structures.location: Enters femoral triangle at mid-inguinal point (halfway between ASIS and pubic symphysis); descends in adductor canal (under sartorius); passes through adductor hiatus at lower third of thigh
structures.clinicalNotes: NAVL mnemonic in femoral triangle (lateral to medial): Nerve, Artery, Vein, Lymphatics (empty space). Common site for arterial access (cardiac catheterisation, IABP). Femoral pseudoaneurysm after catheterisation. Peripheral arterial disease: ABI <0.9 significant. Femoral endarterectomy for occlusive disease.

structures.name: Femoral Nerve
structures.function: Motor to quadriceps femoris, sartorius, pectineus; sensory to anterior and medial thigh; saphenous nerve (terminal branch) provides sensory to medial leg and foot
structures.location: Largest branch of lumbar plexus (L2-L4); emerges lateral to psoas, descends between psoas and iliacus; passes under inguinal ligament lateral to femoral artery; divides into anterior and posterior divisions
structures.clinicalNotes: Femoral nerve block: for hip and knee surgery, analgesia for femoral shaft fracture. FICB (fascia iliaca compartment block). Femoral neuropathy from psoas haematoma (anticoagulants), retractors in hip arthroplasty, diabetic amyotrophy. Saphenous nerve at risk in stripping of great saphenous vein or medial knee incisions.

structures.name: Sciatic Nerve
structures.function: Largest nerve in the body; motor to hamstrings and all leg/foot muscles; sensory to posterior thigh and entire leg below knee (via tibial and common peroneal divisions)
structures.location: Arises from sacral plexus L4-S3; exits pelvis through greater sciatic foramen below piriformis; descends deep to gluteus maximus; lies on short external rotators; divides into tibial and common peroneal nerves at apex of popliteal fossa
structures.bloodSupply: Inferior gluteal artery and popliteal artery branches
structures.clinicalNotes: Sciatica: L4/L5/S1 disc prolapse → dermatomal pain, positive SLR. Piriformis syndrome: mimic of sciatica. Sciatic nerve block for below-knee surgery. At risk in posterior hip replacement, intramuscular injections in gluteal region (upper outer quadrant safe zone). Hamstring injuries at ischial tuberosity.

structures.name: Great Saphenous Vein
structures.function: Longest vein in the body; superficial venous drainage of medial leg and thigh; drains into femoral vein at saphenofemoral junction (SFJ) 4 cm below and lateral to pubic tubercle
structures.location: Starts anterior to medial malleolus; ascends medial side of leg and thigh; passes through the cribriform fascia of the femoral triangle to join femoral vein
structures.clinicalNotes: Varicose veins: SFJ and perforator incompetence → saphenous stripping, EVLA, foam sclerotherapy. Coronary artery bypass graft conduit (reversed long saphenous). Venous cut-down at medial malleolus for emergency IV access. Saphenous nerve injury during stripping causes medial ankle paraesthesia. DVT in deep, not superficial system.

structures.name: Quadriceps Femoris
structures.function: Four-headed muscle group; sole extensor of knee; rectus femoris also flexes hip; patella is sesamoid bone within quadriceps tendon; patellar tendon inserts into tibial tuberosity
structures.location: Rectus femoris (ASIS + ilium), vastus lateralis (lateral femur), vastus medialis (medial femur — VMO important for patellar tracking), vastus intermedius (anterior femur); all converge into quadriceps tendon
structures.bloodSupply: Femoral artery branches, profunda femoris, lateral circumflex femoral
structures.clinicalNotes: Quadriceps tear: sudden deceleration → palpable gap above patella, inability to straight-leg raise. Patellofemoral syndrome: VMO weakness → lateral patellar maltracking. Patella fracture from direct blow or eccentric contraction. Quadriceps strengthening key in ACL rehabilitation. Knee reflex (L3-L4) tests quadriceps.

structures.name: Popliteal Artery
structures.function: Continuation of superficial femoral artery through adductor hiatus; deepest structure in popliteal fossa; divides into anterior and posterior tibial arteries at lower border of popliteus
structures.location: Runs through popliteal fossa between femoral condyles; surrounded by popliteal vein (posterior) and tibial nerve (most superficial); gives genicular branches to knee joint
structures.clinicalNotes: Popliteal aneurysm: commonest peripheral aneurysm; bilateral in 50%; thrombosis → acute ischaemia. Popliteal entrapment syndrome: medial head gastrocnemius compresses artery → claudication in young athletes. Posterior approach for popliteal bypass. Pulse assessment in peripheral arterial disease. Baker's cyst communicates with knee joint (not popliteal artery).

structures.name: Common Peroneal Nerve
structures.function: Branch of sciatic nerve; winds around fibular neck; divides into superficial peroneal (evertor muscles, dorsum of foot sensation) and deep peroneal (dorsiflexors, 1st web space sensation)
structures.location: Separates from sciatic at apex of popliteal fossa; winds around neck of fibula; passes through peroneus longus; divides into superficial and deep branches
structures.clinicalNotes: Most commonly injured peripheral nerve in lower limb. Foot drop: injury at fibular neck (plaster cast pressure, prolonged squatting, lateral knee dislocation, fibular fracture). Deep peroneal palsy: foot drop + 1st web space sensory loss. AFO brace for foot drop. Peroneal nerve block at fibular head.

structures.name: Inguinal Ligament
structures.function: Rolled-under inferior free edge of external oblique aponeurosis; extends from ASIS to pubic tubercle; forms floor of inguinal canal; lacunar ligament (medial expansion) forms medial wall of femoral ring
structures.location: Runs from anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to pubic tubercle; marks boundary between abdomen and thigh; femoral sheath (containing artery, vein, canal) passes under it
structures.bloodSupply: Superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric arteries
structures.clinicalNotes: Femoral hernia: through femoral canal medial to femoral vein, below inguinal ligament — more common in women; high risk of strangulation; repair by McVay (Cooper's ligament) or Lichtenstein approach. Inguinal hernia is above inguinal ligament. Sportsman's hernia: chronic groin pain from inguinal ligament tear. Femoral ring boundaries: anteriorly inguinal ligament.

structures.name: Gastrocnemius
structures.function: Powerful plantarflexor of ankle; assists knee flexion via proximal origin; forms the visible calf bulk; together with soleus forms the triceps surae; inserts via Achilles tendon
structures.location: Two heads: medial (larger, from medial femoral condyle) and lateral (lateral condyle); forms proximal calf; joins soleus to form Achilles tendon inserting into calcaneus
structures.clinicalNotes: Gastrocnemius tear ('tennis leg'): medial head at musculotendinous junction — sudden calf pain, may mimic DVT. Gastrocnemius flap: most reliable local flap for knee and upper third leg wounds. Silfverskjold test differentiates gastrocnemius vs combined triceps surae tightness. Ankle reflex tests S1-S2 via tibial nerve.

structures.name: Femoral Triangle
structures.function: Fascial space in upper thigh containing femoral artery, vein, nerve, deep inguinal lymph nodes; provides access to femoral neurovascular bundle; boundaries: inguinal ligament (base), adductor longus (medial), sartorius (lateral)
structures.location: Floor: iliopsoas laterally and pectineus/adductor longus medially; roof: fascia lata; apex points downward into adductor canal; contains NAVEL contents (Nerve Artery Vein Empty space Lymphatics) lateral to medial
structures.clinicalNotes: Femoral triangle is a key landmark for vascular access, femoral nerve block, and inguinal lymph node biopsy. Femoral hernia exits through femoral canal (medial to vein, below inguinal ligament). Saphena varix: dilated great saphenous vein at SFJ mimics femoral hernia (disappears on lying). Cough impulse distinguishes hernia from other masses.
